04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Fiona Bell's attachment was the first review-procedure sheet Emma had obtained rather than merely heard described. It was a printed guidance sheet for the Glenarraidh Education Trust's 2011 student travel scheme, released because it contained no identifiable applicant information. The separate folder bearing the heading Appeals and reviews had still not been opened.

Emma placed the guidance beside the September press cuttings. Unsuccessful applicants, it stated, could seek reconsideration by writing to the trust within fourteen days of receiving a decision. A reviewer who had not participated in the initial selection was to examine the request. The provisions were clear enough as aspirations. Their implementation was another matter.

The sheet named no reviewer. It specified neither the method of appointment nor what record should be kept of a review outcome. Emma resisted calling the omission evidence of a flawed process. Those details might have appeared in another document. For now, she could establish only that this sheet did not contain them.

“Does that finally tell us there were appeals?” Sarah asked over the telephone.

“It tells us a review mechanism was described. Nothing about whether it was invoked.”

Sarah suggested the parent's published complaint might have been one. Emma looked back at the letter. Its author had objected to the lack of transparency in choosing students, but had mentioned no rejection notice, formal submission or reconsidered decision. A grievance voiced publicly was not necessarily a procedural appeal. Equating the two would convert a possibility into a fact.

Emma opened a fourth column in her notes: Notification. A review right of which eligible applicants had never been informed might exist formally yet be difficult to exercise. Conversely, a dissatisfied parent might know the rules and choose to complain to a newspaper instead. The document could not decide between those scenarios.

Neither could it settle the figures that had brought her here. The article published on 16 September 2011 had reported eight students selected, and the subsequent correction had withdrawn that figure without replacement. The review procedure addressed unsuccessful decisions; it offered no headcount, payment schedule or list of successful beneficiaries. One documentary gap could not be filled by material designed for another purpose.

That afternoon Fiona called. Her colleagues had identified several folders within the student travel box, but the appeals folder remained unopened pending a careful inventory. She could not say whether it contained requests, blank templates or something unrelated. Emma asked instead about records showing who was appointed to consider reviews and whether applicants received the guidance sheet. Fiona promised only to pass on those questions.

Emma checked the document's footer. The sheet was dated August 2011, before the selection announcement, Claire's interview with Emma and the later disappearance. Its date gave the procedure a place in the chronology. It did not show distribution, compliance or awareness.

Sarah sent a short message asking whether the newsroom could describe a right to appeal. Emma revised the proposed wording: The scheme's written guidance provided for reconsideration of rejected applications; the extent to which the procedure was communicated or used has not been established.

She reread it. Restrained language sometimes sounded less dramatic than a mystery deserved. It was also the only language the evidence warranted.

Her next question was not whether a particular student had complained. It was more basic, and potentially more revealing: How, in September 2011, were applicants told that the review procedure existed?
